cards.b: The Bennets of Longbourn have five girls and an estate entailed to a male cousin. When Mr. Bennet dies, the family loses its home. So Mrs. Bennet has one mission: marry her daughters well. Then a rich bachelor, Mr. Bingley, rents the house next door.

At the local ball, Bingley falls for gentle Jane. His friend Darcy, even richer and far colder, refuses to dance with Elizabeth and calls her merely tolerable within her hearing. She laughs it off. But that single remark shapes everything she believes about him.

cards.t: A charming man tells a convenient story
cards.b: Handsome officer George Wickham tells Elizabeth that Darcy cheated him of an inheritance. She believes every word, because it confirms what she already feels. Meanwhile Bingley leaves suddenly for London, and Jane is quietly heartbroken.

cards.t: The worst proposal in English literature
cards.b: In Kent, Darcy suddenly declares his love, while dwelling on how far beneath him her family is. Elizabeth refuses him with fury. She accuses him of wrecking Jane's happiness and ruining Wickham, and says no manner of his could have won her.

Darcy answers in writing. He explains he thought Jane didn't care for Bingley, and reveals the truth about Wickham: a spendthrift who tried to elope with Darcy's fifteen-year-old sister for her fortune. Elizabeth rereads it until she sees her own blindness.

cards.q: Till this moment I never knew myself.
cards.b: Elizabeth, after reading Darcy's letter. The cleverest person in the book realizes her judgment was driven by vanity.

Touring Derbyshire, Elizabeth visits Darcy's estate, Pemberley, believing him away. His housekeeper praises him as the kindest master alive. Then Darcy appears, gracious and warm, and treats her uncle from trade with real respect. He has taken her words to heart.

Lydia, the youngest Bennet, runs off with Wickham, threatening to disgrace the whole family. Darcy quietly tracks them down, pays Wickham's debts and arranges the marriage, then insists no one be told. Elizabeth learns the truth by accident.

Bingley returns and marries Jane. Darcy's aunt, Lady Catherine, storms in to forbid a match with Elizabeth, who refuses to promise anything. That gives Darcy hope. He proposes again, humbly, and this time she says yes.

Witty, independent and fearless with powerful people. Her flaw is pride in her own perceptiveness: she trusts her quick reads of people and builds clever arguments to defend them. Her growth is learning to doubt herself.
Honorable, loyal and generous, hidden behind class snobbery and social awkwardness. His growth is learning that good manners are owed to everyone, not only to people of his rank.

Austen shows every kind: the Bennets (attraction without respect), Charlotte and Mr. Collins (security without love), Lydia and Wickham (impulse without sense). Against them she sets Jane and Elizabeth, whose marriages rest on affection and esteem.

cards.t: Both of them are proud. Both are prejudiced.
cards.b: It is tempting to cast Darcy as pride and Elizabeth as prejudice. Austen gives each both. His pride in rank creates prejudice against her family; her pride in her judgment creates prejudice against him.

cards.t: Money is real, but not enough
cards.b: Austen never pretends money doesn't matter. Women of the gentry had almost no other route to security. Yet the book shows that marrying for money alone, or for attraction alone, leads to unhappiness.

cards.t: Rank is not the same as worth
cards.b: Lady Catherine has the highest title and the worst manners. The Gardiners, who earn their living in trade, are the most truly well-bred people in the story. Character comes from conduct, not birth.
Austen's first title for the novel was First Impressions. Elizabeth's whole mistake grows from one overheard remark. A first impression is a piece of data, not a verdict.

cards.t: Be suspicious of stories you want to believe
cards.b: Elizabeth never asks why a near-stranger shares such private grievances so fast. When a story flatters what you already feel, that is the moment to check it hardest.
Clever people can build better excuses for wrong conclusions. Elizabeth's wit made her mistake more convincing, not less. Self-knowledge is the real safeguard.
Both lovers are changed by harsh words from the other. Each could have stayed defensive. Instead they asked whether the criticism was true, and grew.

cards.t: Change shows in what you do
cards.b: Darcy never announces he has reformed. He simply behaves better, and rescues Lydia without wanting credit. Judge growth, in others and yourself, by conduct when no one is keeping score.
Mr. Bennet's ironic detachment is charming on the page and disastrous in life. Lydia's elopement is the cost of years of avoided responsibility.
Neither could love the other while each was sure of being right. The happy ending arrives only after both admit they were wrong.
Whom have you judged on a first impression? What would it take for you to read their side of the letter?

On Manor Farm, the prize boar Old Major gathers the animals one night. Humans, he says, steal the fruits of animal labor and kill them when they're no longer useful. He dreams of a world without masters, teaches them a rousing anthem, and dies three nights later.

The farmer, Mr. Jones, is a neglectful drunk. One day he forgets to feed the animals, and they break into the store shed. Furious and hungry, they drive Jones and his men off the farm. They rename it Animal Farm and celebrate their freedom.

cards.t: Seven rules on the barn wall
cards.b: The cleverest pigs, Snowball and Napoleon, turn Old Major's ideas into a system called Animalism. They paint Seven Commandments on the barn: no animal shall wear clothes, sleep in a bed, drink alcohol or kill another animal, and all animals are equal.

The first harvest is the best ever, and the animals work joyfully. But the cows' milk quietly disappears, and so do the windfall apples. The pigs' spokesman, Squealer, explains that pigs need them for brainwork. Without them, he warns, Jones might come back. No one argues.

Snowball, a brilliant speaker, champions a windmill to bring electricity and shorter workdays. Napoleon opposes it. At the decisive meeting, Napoleon whistles, and nine huge dogs he secretly raised from puppies chase Snowball off the farm. Napoleon abolishes the meetings.

Days later, Napoleon announces the windmill was his idea all along. The animals work brutally hard to build it. When a storm wrecks it, Napoleon blames the absent Snowball. From then on, every failure, broken egg and missing item is blamed on the traitor.

Napoleon stages a purge. Animals confess to plotting with Snowball and the dogs tear their throats out on the spot. The survivors huddle in shock. When they check the barn wall, the rule against killing now says no animal shall kill another without cause.

cards.t: The horse who worked himself to death
cards.b: Boxer, the strongest and most loyal horse, answers every hardship by working harder and trusting Napoleon. When he collapses, the pigs say he's going to a hospital. The van that takes him belongs to a horse slaughterer. Squealer insists it was a misunderstanding.

cards.t: Pig and man, side by side
cards.b: Years pass. The pigs walk on two legs, wear clothes, drink whisky and sleep in beds. The Commandments are replaced by a single rule. At a dinner with neighboring farmers, the watching animals look from pig to man and can no longer tell which is which.

cards.q: All animals are equal, but some are more equal than others.
cards.b: A paraphrase of the single rule that replaces the Commandments. Orwell turns the revolution's founding promise into a joke that exposes the new ruling class.

Napoleon is a quiet, ruthless schemer who wins through force and secrecy; he stands for Stalin. Snowball is an energetic idealist with real ideas, recast as a villain after his exile; he stands for Trotsky. Orwell suggests neither offered the animals real freedom.

Squealer can make black seem white. He uses statistics, false memories and fear of Jones's return to justify every betrayal. He represents propaganda, and he's often the most chilling character because he never needs violence. Words do his work.

Boxer's mottoes are to work harder and that Napoleon is always right; his loyalty is exploited to the end. Benjamin the donkey sees everything and does nothing. The sheep drown out debate with chanted slogans. Each shows a way ordinary people enable tyranny.

The pigs never seize total control in one move. They take the milk, then the decisions, then the rules, then lives. Each step seems small and is explained away. Orwell shows that tyranny usually grows through accepted exceptions.

The Commandments are quietly rewritten at night. History is edited so Snowball was always a traitor. The animals can't read well and can't remember clearly, so they can't prove anything changed. Language and memory become tools of control.

Orwell, a socialist, wrote the book as a warning about the Soviet Union. His point isn't that change is pointless. It's that a revolution which hands power to a new elite, without accountability, ends by recreating the oppression it overthrew.

The milk and apples were the first sign. When the people in charge grant themselves a small privilege and explain it away, ask what it will become. Big abuses usually start as reasonable-sounding exceptions.
The pigs got away with rewriting the rules because no one kept a record. In a workplace, a group or a country, written commitments and good memory are protection. Keep the receipts.
Boxer's virtue, unquestioning devotion, became the instrument of his death. Loyalty to people or causes is admirable, but it has to be loyalty to what they do, not only to what they say.
Benjamin understood what was happening and stayed silent, saying nothing would ever change. Seeing clearly is only half the job. Knowledge that never becomes action changes nothing.

Every failure on the farm was blamed on Snowball, and the threat of Jones returning ended every argument. When leaders explain all problems through an enemy, it's often to avoid explaining their own decisions.
The sheep chant whenever debate begins, and the chant always wins. Simple slogans feel like clarity but often shut down the questions that matter. When a phrase replaces an argument, slow down.
The animals won their freedom in a single afternoon and lost it over years of inattention. Rights are kept by people who keep paying attention, keep asking questions and keep meeting together.
Where in your own life do you rely on someone else's account of what was agreed? Which character would you honestly have been on Animal Farm?

cards.t: A boy, a graveyard, a convict
cards.b: On the Kentish marshes, little orphan Pip is visiting his parents' graves when an escaped convict seizes him and demands food and a file. Terrified, Pip steals both from the home of his harsh sister and her husband, gentle Joe the blacksmith. When soldiers recapture the man, he claims he stole the food himself, quietly shielding the boy.

Pip is summoned to play at Satis House, home of the rich, strange Miss Havisham. Jilted on her wedding day, she still wears the yellowed dress, the clocks frozen at twenty to nine, the cake rotting on the table. Her ward, the beautiful Estella, mocks Pip's coarse hands and thick boots. He goes home ashamed of everything he is.

Pip becomes Joe's apprentice, the life he once looked forward to, but now the forge feels like a prison. His sister is struck down by an unseen attacker, likely the sullen journeyman Orlick, and left disabled. Kind, clever Biddy comes to help the household. Pip confides to her that he wants to be a gentleman, chiefly to win Estella.

The formidable London lawyer Mr. Jaggers appears with astonishing news: an anonymous benefactor will make Pip a gentleman of great expectations. Pip must never ask who. He is certain it is Miss Havisham, grooming him to marry Estella. He leaves the forge for London, and is already a little embarrassed by Joe as he says goodbye.

In London Pip shares rooms with cheerful Herbert Pocket, learns manners, joins a club of idle young men, and runs up debts. When Joe visits in his Sunday clothes, Pip is cold and mortified. Joe leaves with perfect dignity, saying they are simply not meant to be together in London. Pip knows he has behaved badly, and does it anyway.

On a stormy night a weathered old man climbs to Pip's rooms. It is the convict from the marshes, Abel Magwitch. Transported to Australia, he grew rich as a sheep farmer and sent every penny to the boy who once fed him. Miss Havisham had nothing to do with it. And returning to England means the gallows for Magwitch.

cards.q: Yes, Pip, dear boy, I've made a gentleman on you! It's me wot has done it!
cards.b: Magwitch, revealing himself as the secret benefactor. In one sentence Pip's dream of refinement is traced back to the man he most wanted to forget.

The truths tumble out. Miss Havisham's faithless bridegroom, Compeyson, was Magwitch's old criminal partner and enemy. Estella turns out to be Magwitch's own daughter, her mother the housekeeper in Jaggers's kitchen. Estella marries the brutish Bentley Drummle. Miss Havisham finally sees the harm she has done and begs forgiveness, then her dress catches fire; Pip burns his hands saving her.

Pip, Herbert and their friend Startop row Magwitch down the Thames to meet a steamer abroad. Compeyson has betrayed them, and a police boat intercepts. In the struggle Compeyson drowns and Magwitch is badly injured, then condemned to death. Pip, no longer ashamed of him, sits by his bed daily and tells him at the end that his daughter lives and Pip loves her.

Penniless and gravely ill, Pip is nursed back to health by Joe, who quietly pays his debts. Pip returns to propose to Biddy, only to find her marrying Joe, and humbly asks their forgiveness. He works abroad with Herbert for eleven years. Back at the ruins of Satis House he meets the widowed Estella, softened by suffering, and they leave together.

cards.t: Pip: the narrator who judges himself
cards.b: Pip tells the story as an older man looking back, and he is merciless about his younger self. His snobbery, ingratitude and self-deception are all on display. That honesty is the book's quiet miracle: we watch a decent boy turn into a vain young man, and then watch the grown man take full responsibility for him.

Joe cannot read well, speaks clumsily and is happiest at his forge, yet he is the finest person in the novel. He shields Pip from his sister's temper, forgives every slight, and arrives without reproach when Pip falls. Dickens makes the point plainly: gentleness of heart, not polish or money, is what makes a gentleman.

cards.t: Miss Havisham: grief turned to revenge
cards.b: Abandoned at the altar, Miss Havisham stopped every clock and raised Estella as a weapon to break men's hearts. She is gothic and grotesque, but also pitiful: she has wasted her life nursing one wound. Her late, anguished cry of remorse is among the most moving moments in Dickens, because it comes when she can no longer undo anything.

Victorian England sorted people by birth, money and manners. Pip believes rising in class will make him worthy of Estella. Dickens turns that upside down: the convict Magwitch is generous, the blacksmith Joe is noble, and the polished gentleman Compeyson is a swindler. Real worth is moral, not social, and Pip learns it at great cost.

From the stolen pie onward, Pip carries a heavy, half-hidden guilt. Some is irrational, a child's terror; some is fully earned, as in his treatment of Joe and Biddy. The novel tracks how a conscience grows: Pip begins by fearing he will be caught and ends by actually making amends to the people he wronged.

cards.t: The past that will not let go
cards.b: Satis House is the novel's great image of a life frozen by one injury. But almost everyone is bound to the past: Magwitch to a boy's kindness, Pip to the marsh he tries to forget, Estella to her upbringing. The question Dickens poses is whether we can be shaped by what happened without being imprisoned by it.

cards.t: Never be ashamed of who raised you
cards.b: Pip's worst moment is not a crime but a snub: hiding his embarrassment at Joe's clothes and grammar while Joe sits in his London rooms. Joe's love was the best thing Pip ever had. When success makes you wince at the people who stood by you first, the problem is not them, and it is worth fixing now.

A frightened boy hands a starving man some bread, cheese and a pork pie. Years later, that act returns as an entire fortune. Dickens exaggerates, but the truth holds: you rarely know which ordinary act of decency will matter most to someone. Treat the small, unwatched kindnesses as if they count, because they often do.

cards.t: Question the story that flatters you
cards.b: Pip assumes Miss Havisham is his patron because it fits his dearest wish: Estella and refinement, all arranged for him. He never tests the idea, and it shapes years of choices. When an explanation makes you the hero of a romance, that is exactly when to look harder at the evidence.

Miss Havisham tried to freeze the moment she was hurt, and decades later she is still in it, surrounded by decay. Holding on to a grievance can feel like loyalty to yourself. In fact it lets the person who hurt you keep running your life. Grieve fully, then let the clocks start again.

Miss Havisham trained Estella to break hearts as revenge on all men, and succeeded so well that Estella could not love even her. Whatever we teach children or those who depend on us, they will carry. Pass on your wounds, and you don't heal them; you multiply them, often against yourself.

cards.t: Don't spend money you're only expecting
cards.b: Pip and Herbert live on future riches, running up bills and holding solemn evenings to list their debts, which somehow makes them feel prudent. When the expectations vanish, the debts remain. Living on what you hope to get rather than what you have is a trap that only looks like optimism.

cards.t: Use good fortune to lift a friend
cards.b: The one wholly good thing Pip does with his money is to secretly buy Herbert a partnership in a shipping firm. It later becomes Pip's own livelihood. Wealth that only polishes our image fades quickly; wealth quietly turned into someone else's opportunity is the part that lasts, and often comes back.

After his fall, Pip goes back to Joe and Biddy and asks their forgiveness plainly, with no defence of his past self. They give it at once. Pride makes apologies feel like losing. Pip shows the opposite: owning a wrong completely is how he finally becomes the kind of man he wanted to be.

Whose quiet support helped make you who you are, perhaps someone you have outgrown, drifted from, or felt embarrassed by, the way Pip felt about Joe? What would it take to let them know today what they meant to you?
